sources.news_title: Dems express ‘points of anxiety’ over Trump’s summit with Putin and Xi
sources.text:
Dems express ‘points of anxiety’ over Trump’s summit with Putin and Xi
GOP lawmakers see president trying to ‘make sure we don't end up at war’
President Donald Trump prepares to shake hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)
Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of issues even as he appears politically weakened at home.
Trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal. But before he left, Trump signaled the three-way talks also likely would include the artificial intelligence race, Moscow’s bloody war with Ukraine, global trade and his standoff with Iran.
The U.S. commander in chief’s tendency to sound deferential to Putin and habit of referring to Xi as a personal “friend” concerns many congressional Democrats. But Trump’s GOP allies on Capitol Hill, despite this month’s midterm election losses, still describe him as a dealmaker who has a chance to use his final years to bend Putin and Xi toward U.S. interests.
Rick Scott, a Florida Republican who sits on the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said Tuesday he was hopeful that Trump could make some progress on at least one issue with the Russian and Chinese leaders.
“As we all know, China and Russia want to destroy our way of life,” he said. “But it would be great to reduce … nuclear stockpiles and make sure we're not going to ever get attacked.
Still, Scott sounded skeptical about two world leaders Trump has tried to keep close during his two terms. “But do I trust Xi or Putin? No, they're a bunch of liars.” Asked if he worries Trump might trust them too much, Scott replied: “I don't think he trusts him any more than I do. … I'm glad the president's trying. Hope springs eternal. But do I actually really believe something good's going to come out of it? I don't.”
Outgoing House Armed Services Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., said part of Trump’s talks on Thursday “should be to make sure the world is a safer place, to make sure we don't have aggressive behavior like Russia in an unprovoked attack against Ukraine.
“They ought to be talking about how they don't do those sorts of things, how they don't threaten their neighbors, how they don't try to intimidate through the assertion of force that they ought to be able to work together to make sure we assure a safe globe,” said Wittman, who lost his reelection race earlier this month.
That comment came one day after Trump told reporters as he left the White House for Asia that he sees Putin “backing down a little bit” in his conduct of the war with Ukraine.
“I think he could be tougher. I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly,” Trump said Monday. “I think he's backing down.”
Those kinds of deferential remarks about the Russian leader are a big reason why some Democrats have heartburn about Thursday’s meeting.
Senate Armed Services member Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said Tuesday that she’s concerned about the Shenzhen summit because “I’m not sure what’s going to pop out of [Trump’s] mouth next — especially for a meeting with two guys he clearly likes.”
Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., also a member of the Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said he has “high hopes” for the trilateral meeting — but “maybe not high expectations.”
“I have some points of anxiety. I'm nervous about any discussion about Ukraine that doesn't involve the Ukrainians. And, so, some of the advance to this is like, ‘We're going to talk about ending the Ukraine war.’ You can't do that without Ukraine at the table,” Kaine said. “So the desire to bring about more peace and stability, that's a good thing to talk about. But no conditions about Ukraine and ending that war without them at the table? Not so sure about that.”
During remarks Tuesday on the Senate floor, Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer criticized what he described as Trump’s misplaced priorities.
“Enforcement of the new rules restricting China’s access to our most sensitive AI chips should start today,” the New York Democrat said, adding that Trump should focus more of his Asia swing on securing commitments from U.S. allies to block China from gaining an upper hand in the AI technology race.
Trump touted just that on Tuesday during remarks in Manila at a U.S.-Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in the Philippines.
“Since I returned to office, we've made major trade deals with Malaysia, Cambodia, Indonesia, as well as Japan, South Korea, and almost everybody, frankly, at the table,” he said. “And we've made many other vital agreements across the region spanning energy, critical minerals and technology.”
But on Wednesday, Trump appeared to have pivoted to the trip’s main event.
He stood beside Xi at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen and smiled as Putin approached. Trump extended his hand and shook Putin’s as the Chinese leader looked on.
Scott, a Trump ally in the Senate, said Tuesday he sees the president “trying to build relationships to try to make sure we don't end up at war [because] he doesn't like war.”
Trump signaled Monday that he might press Xi for details on an alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, costing the AI mogul his job as the company’s president and CEO. He also said he could bring up Nvidia’s sales of sophisticated microchips that many lawmakers — Republican and Democrat — want to ensure remain in the U.S. for domestic AI development.
The administration’s response to the turmoil at Nvidia, with Trump even suggesting he'd support Huang returning as CEO, is a rare area where Republicans have expressed concern publicly. House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie, R-Kent., wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Wednesday seeking information about “the implementation of federal laws governing technology exports, in particular the application of export controls relating to semiconductor chips, the effect of which has a broad impact on America’s race with China to artificial intelligence (AI) dominance and the ability of U.S. companies to set global technology standards.”
Heather Williams, director of the Project on Nuclear Issues at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote this week that for the three leaders, the “path is fraught with challenges.”
“Putin could diplomatically outmaneuver the Trump administration and make any progress on nuclear issues dependent on undermining Western support to Ukraine,” she wrote in an analysis for the Washington, D.C.-based think tank. “Even the optics of Trump and Putin negotiating while the war continues and as Russia ramps up missile strikes on Ukrainian civilian targets could be interpreted as undermining U.S. values.”

sources.news_title: Trump, Xi, Putin meet at APEC in summit that could reshape global balance of power
sources.text:
The leaders of the United States, China, and Russia are preparing for a historic trilateral summit in Shenzhen on Thursday, a meeting that could have important implications for the future of the international order.
US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin are expected to discuss nuclear weapons, the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and the broader balance of power among the world’s leading countries.
Trump’s visit to China is symbolic and is part of a tradition of US-China talks that date back to the last century. US President Richard Nixon visited the People’s Republic of China for a week in February 1972. His visit came against the backdrop of the Cold War and détente.
Nixon was the first sitting US president to travel to mainland China, ending over two decades of diplomatic isolation between Washington and Beijing. His national security advisor, Henry Kissinger, made a secret trip to Beijing in July 1971 to meet with premier Zhou Enlai.
Since then, more US presidents have visited China: Gerald Ford in 1975, Ronald Reagan in 1984, George H.W. Bush in 1989, and Bill Clinton in 1998.
China seeks greater global influence amid wars and shifting power dynamics
George W. Bush traveled to China numerous times as US-China ties appeared to be growing even more important. He went at least four times from 2001-2008. This was followed by several visits by Barack Obama and also two previous trips by Trump, one in his first term and one this past May.
China has changed immensely in that time. It has gone far beyond a doctrine of “hide your strength, bide your time,” a feature of Deng Xiaoping’s reform era in the 1980s and early 1990s and of his successor, Jiang Zemin.
That has been replaced by what some see as China’s more aggressive policies these days, as it seeks to take up the mantle of global leadership.
China’s rapidly expanding navy is a sign of its growing power. Like the Royal Navy and then the US Navy in the early 20th Century, China is becoming a global naval power with a trend that could upend the US-led global order.
The current summit in China is taking place alongside the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meetings, which China is also hosting in Shenzhen. The gathering provides Beijing with an opportunity to present itself as a central player in international diplomacy and economic cooperation.
Chinese state media has emphasized the importance of the occasion. The three leaders would hold an in-depth exchange of views on important issues concerning global peace, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Wednesday, China’s official Xinhua News Agency reported.
The meeting comes at a time when the international system is under increasing strain. The war involving the US, Israel, and Iran has disrupted energy markets and maritime trade.
Russia’s war in Ukraine continues to divide Moscow and Western countries, while tensions between Washington and Beijing have raised questions about the future of trade, technology, and security in the Indo-Pacific.
China sees these wars as accelerating global change. This is not just about a multipolar world order. This is about how China believes it can step into the power vacuum that may be left by a decline of the US or Russia.
For Trump, the summit offers an opportunity to pursue agreements with two of America’s principal strategic competitors. For Xi, it is a chance to demonstrate China’s growing international influence. Putin, meanwhile, can use the meeting to reinforce Russia’s status as a major power whose interests must be considered in discussions about global security.
China presents its vision of international cooperation. It has sought to frame the Shenzhen meetings around openness, innovation, and economic integration.
On Wednesday, Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, hosted a banquet welcoming international leaders attending APEC. He described Shenzhen as an example of China’s economic transformation and its engagement with the wider world, Xinhua reported. Openness was deeply rooted in the city’s identity, while innovation and cooperation had contributed to its success, he said.
APEC had helped make the Asia-Pacific one of the world’s most dynamic economic regions, Xi said at the APEC Summit. He called for greater regional integration and cooperation among governments and businesses.
The APEC gathering brought together more than 2,000 representatives from more than 30 economies, including Britain, France, Germany, and Switzerland, Xinhua reported.
The economic importance of the region is substantial. APEC economies account for about 40% of the world’s population, more than 60% of global GDP, and nearly half of international trade.
These figures illustrate why the summit matters beyond the relationship among Washington, Beijing, and Moscow. Decisions affecting trade, investment, technology, and security in the Asia-Pacific can have consequences for the global economy.
Xi, Putin promote multipolar world order ahead of trilateral summit
China and Russia are also promoting a multipolar world. Xi met with Putin in Shenzhen on Wednesday, ahead of the trilateral summit. He said China-Russia relations had brought greater stability and certainty to a world experiencing turbulence and transformation, Xinhua reported.
Xi highlighted two anniversaries: 30 years since the establishment of the China-Russia strategic partnership of coordination; and 25 years since the signing of their Treaty of Good-Neighborliness and Friendly Cooperation.
The relationship was an example of cooperation between major powers based on equality, mutual respect, and shared interests, he said.
Xi also called on China and Russia to deepen cooperation and promote a multipolar world and what Beijing describes as the democratization of international relations.
This language is significant because China and Russia have increasingly advocated an international system in which American influence is balanced by other major powers.
Their vision contrasts with the US-led international order that emerged after the Cold War. China and Russia also have different interests, however, and their cooperation does not eliminate competition or disagreements between them.
Xi personally welcomed Trump at Shenzhen Bao’an International Airport on Wednesday. They was an elaborate reception involving military honors, national anthems, and Chinese fighter jets flying overhead, Xinhua reported. It was a reprise of the flyover when XI visited the US this past September.
At Joint Base Andrews during Xi’s arrival, two B-1B Lancer bombers flew overhead during the arrival ceremony and national anthem after Trump and First Lady Melania Trump greeted Xi and his wife on the tarmac. The overflight made a huge roar.
On Wednesday, Xi recalled his visit to the US and said he hoped to discuss bilateral relations, Asia-Pacific cooperation, and the wider international landscape. He appeared to be quietly referencing the flyover as well, Xinhua reported.
Trump thanked Xi for the reception and praised China and its leader, the report said.
Nuclear arms control expected to dominate Trump, Xi, Putin summit
An issue expected to dominate Thursday’s trilateral summit is nuclear arms control. Trump has expressed interest in reducing nuclear weapons and potentially establishing new restrictions involving the world’s three leading nuclear powers, UAE-based news site Al-Ain News reported.
The wars in Iran and Ukraine illustrate why the summit will impact the international order. China is a major consumer of Middle Eastern energy trade, including from Iran in the past, and has a direct economic interest in restoring stability to the Gulf and protecting maritime trade. Russia also has a history of involvement in negotiations concerning Iran’s nuclear program.
Trump has indicated that the wars in Iran and Ukraine could both be raised during the summit, despite earlier indications from American officials that Ukraine would not be on the formal agenda, Al-Ain News reported.
What if China seeks a role in diplomatic efforts involving both conflicts? This remains to be seen.
European officials were worried Trump might make concessions concerning Ukraine, the Al-Ain News report said, citing US news site Axios. European governments fear that decisions affecting their security could be discussed without their direct participation, the report said.
The significance of the Shenzhen summit will be seen in the months ahead.
For decades since the end of the Cold War, the US has led the international system. China’s economic and military rise, Russia’s confrontation with the West, and the growing importance of regional powers have challenged that arrangement.
Xi and Putin are explicitly promoting a multipolar order. Trump, meanwhile, has demonstrated an interest in negotiating directly with other powerful leaders on nuclear weapons, regional conflicts, and other pressing issues.
The three countries do not share a common vision of international security. The summit could establish a precedent for regular consultations among them.
For China, hosting the meeting reinforces its claim to a central role in global diplomacy. For Russia, participation demonstrates that Moscow remains an important player in decisions affecting international security. For Trump, the summit offers an opportunity to pursue agreements that could reshape relations among the world’s leading powers.
The question is whether the meeting will become the beginning of a more stable international framework or simply another encounter between leaders whose strategic interests remain fundamentally opposed. As the three presidents prepare to meet, the future of international order is at stake.

Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping exchanged handshakes as the world's most powerful men were pictured together for the very first time.
The leaders greeted each other in the Chinese city of Shenzhen as the trio arrived for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit.
The annual gathering sees the leaders of 21 countries from the Pacific region meet to discuss free trade, regional integregation and greater economic cooperation.
The exchange between Mr Trump and Putin marked the first time the pair have met face-to-face since their meeting in Alaska in August 2025.
Kremlin-backed media has hailed the handshake between the Russian and American leaders in front of President Xi as "historic".
The trio were photographed together on the red carpet ahead of a welcome banquet to commence the historic summit.
Tomorrow, they will take part in a historic trilateral meeting for the very first time.
Ahead of the talks, Putin said partnership, rather than isolation, was required, and the summit provided an opportunity for a constructive exchange of views between the global powers.
"I therefore expect big potential benefit from the upcoming trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, China and the United States, which is scheduled to take place on the sidelines of the Apec summit," he said.
A senior aide to Putin, Yury Ushakov, told Russian state media he expects the Russian leader to meet with Mr Trump several times over the coming days.
He said: "The leaders will meet, believe me, and they will have a substantive conversation, regardless of where they happen to be sitting - in armchairs, on chairs or on stools - or standing face-to-face, looking each other in the eye.
"The meeting will take place. Our president and the US president will meet a few times over the course of the summit."
Mr Trump has suggested he wants the war in Ukraine to be the focus of the talks; however Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky cast doubt over whether this will play out.

However, the meeting is widely viewed as a failure as it did not prevent the more than four-decade-long Cold War which followed.

sources.news_title: Trump gets a personal tarmac welcome from Xi after landing in China
sources.text:
Trump gets a personal tarmac welcome from Xi after landing in China
SHENZHEN, China (AP) — President Donald Trump landed in China on Wednesday, seeking to reinforce the U.S. status as the world’s leading technology power, but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left the administration scrambling to calm the American public.
The issues put the administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty ahead of a potentially complicated trilateral meeting on Thursday with the presidents of China and Russia, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
As he began his trip to Asia, Trump initially had been nonchalant about the outages that left people in the United States worried about accessing their email, checking their bank accounts or safely flying on an airplane.
“It’s fine,” Trump pronounced on Tuesday from the Philippine capital of Manila, suggesting it was all just a consequence of being a nation that is “big and powerful.”
But then the outages involving Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration, JPMorgan Chase and the National Security Agency’s communications network began to overshadow Trump’s visit. They raised the specter that artificial intelligence can disrupt daily life, as new cyber vulnerabilities identified require software to be constantly upgraded to fix flaws or other security holes, known as patching, which is supposed to improve how the technology runs.
So at the start of the second day of Trump’s trip, Secretary of State Marco Rubio stepped in to reassure Americans on Trump’s behalf. He told reporters there was “zero” evidence that the outages are connected or tied to rival nations, cyber hackers or criminals.
“Sometimes when you are going in to fix your system because you’ve identified a vulnerability, it creates a short-term disruption,” said Rubio, who is also Trump’s national security adviser.
Trump is trying to project strength in Asia, but the outages challenge that image
Xi paid Trump a special honor by greeting him on the tarmac after Air Force One arrived in Shenzhen, China, reciprocating a gesture made by the U.S. president during Xi’s state visit to Washington in September.
The two leaders greeted each other at the foot of the airplane’s stairs in a handshake that became a hug as group of dancers waved flowers and flags. When Putin arrived earlier on Wednesday, Xi did not greet him at the airport despite their longstanding friendship.
Trump has signaled that he wants to take an improvised approach during his time in Shenzhen, the skyscraper-filled tech hub that is hosting world leaders for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. It’s a bet that his unscripted brand of diplomacy based on personal relationships can create some kind of legacy to reshape world affairs during his final two years in the White House.
The White House said that Trump would have two separate meetings on Wednesday with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney before the official APEC greeting ceremony. Trump has previously voiced his disapproval of the U.S. trade pact with Canada and Mexico that was negotiated during his first term.
As leaders were introduced on Wednesday night ahead of an APEC group photo, Putin approached Trump. They shook hands and traded greetings.
On Thursday, at a first-ever trilateral, Trump said he plans to talk with Xi and Putin about limiting nuclear weapons and bringing an end to the war in Ukraine, which began in 2022 with Russia’s invasion. Analysts are not expecting substantive breakthroughs, despite the unprecedented nature of the meeting.
Before the trip, Trump’s aides had told reporters that the war in Ukraine would not be on the agenda. But Trump said on Tuesday that the deaths of tens of thousands of Russian troops every month had created an opening to resolve the conflict.
“I think it’s very close to getting it done,” Trump said. “We’re going to have a good meeting on that.”
Trump also teased the possibility of a private meeting with Putin and a separate sit-down with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. But neither option had been added to his official schedule.
Trump has a reunion with old friend Imelda Marcos
Before he landed in Shenzhen, Trump had lunch in Manila with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at the Malacañang Presidential Palace.
Marcos noted that he had sent fried chicken from the Philippine chain Jollibee to the U.S. delegation for a late-night snack Tuesday and complimented Trump for “working very hard.”
Trump praised the U.S. bond with the Philippines and the interior decoration of the presidential palace.
“Our people share common history, common values, common interests, common architectural tastes,” Trump said. “I love what you’ve done here.”
He said after their meeting that the two nations had reached a trade deal on Wednesday, though he had also said last year that an agreement had been reached.
Trump also had a short reunion with Imelda Marcos, the former first lady and mother of the Philippines’ current president.
Famed for her lavish shoe collection, Imelda Marcos knew Trump decades ago through the New York City party scene. During the 1986 “People Power” uprising, her husband, Ferdinand Marcos, was ousted as the Philippines’ strongman leader.
Trump called her “always the most beautiful” and the 97-year-old matriarch appeared to hand him a gift, according to a video posted by the White House.
What’s on the agenda for Trump’s meetings with Xi and Putin
The prospect of Trump meeting with two of America’s largest geopolitical rivals has been a source of unease as the U.S. president has been less welcoming of historic allies such as Canada and NATO partners in Europe.
His tariffs that were intended to curb China’s trade surplus have done little to stop the progress of the world’s dominant manufacturer, which for the second straight year will have exported $1 trillion more in goods than what it imported.
Even without the digital outages in the U.S., questions about how to handle AI loom over the summit.
The technology is viewed as key to unlocking faster economic growth, but its rapid development has meant it poses national security risks and could evolve in ways that put AI beyond human control.
Trump’s close tech industry ally Jensen Huang was recently removed as the CEO of Nvidia after he admitted to an affair with a woman alleged to be an agent of the Chinese government. Beijing has denied that she was a spy, yet the affair raised concerns about how China has been able to access Nvidia computer chips to develop its own AI models that are competing with the U.S.
When asked this week why the U.S. had not been more aggressive in cutting off China’s access to advanced computer chips, Trump said there were differences of opinion inside his administration and that “We have a very good relationship with China, and you don’t want to insult them.”
___
Price reported from Manila, Philippines. AP writers Darlene Superville in Washington and Jim Gomez in Manila contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Chinese President Xi embraces Trump at Shenzhen airport
Trump arrives in China for a meeting with historic adversaries
sources.text:
Trump arrives in China for a meeting with historic U.S. adversaries
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- President Trump arrived in Shenzhen for the first summit of the leaders of the United States, Russia and China.
- Trump hopes to discuss nuclear arms control and Iran, while Russia’s Vladimir Putin seeks room to continue the war in Ukraine and Xi Jinping promotes China’s global influence.
SHENZHEN, China — President Trump has begun an extraordinary visit to Shenzhen, where he is set to join the leaders of Russia and China — two of Washington’s principal geopolitical rivals — for an unprecedented trilateral summit Thursday.
Chinese President Xi Jinping personally welcomed Trump on the tarmac upon his arrival, reciprocating a rare honor Trump extended to him during his September visit to Washington.
All three leaders attended a dinner alongside other regional heads of government on Wednesday night, participating in the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, known as APEC.
The trilateral meeting will be the first of its kind by leaders of the United States, Russia and China, three nations with the world’s largest nuclear arsenals.
But while Trump has embraced a strategy of diplomatic engagement with historic foes, the three leaders enter the meeting with starkly different agendas.
Russian President Vladimir Putin hopes to secure space and time to continue executing his war against Ukraine. Trump says he would like to discuss a nuclear arms control agreement and his war in Iran. And Xi aims to present China as a superpower on the international stage, capable of forging world peace.
Meeting with Putin before Trump arrived, Xi said that China’s relationship with Russia had remained as steadfast “as a rock through wind and rain.”
The two sides, he said, would pursue a “multipolar world” — a vision for a global balance of power that would see American influence weakened across Europe and Asia.
A new rule tightening loopholes in U.S. export controls sends a dual message to Beijing ahead of Thursday’s summit.
Trump, for his part, has hedged on his expectations of the summit, signaling resolve against China ahead of his arrival here.
On Monday, the Trump administration tightened export controls on semiconductor chips essential to artificial intelligence development, closing loopholes aimed at curbing Chinese efforts to circumvent restrictions — a move that Trump acknowledged might be an “insult” to Xi before the meeting.
Chinese officials said Wednesday afternoon that Beijing reserved the right to retaliate.
“In essence, the United States is simultaneously trying to find limited avenues of cooperation with China while trying to clamp down on their access to critical parts of the AI supply chain, which doesn’t set up the conditions for productive dialogue,” said Aalok Mehta, director of the Wadhwani AI Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Trump also met in Manila on Tuesday with fellow members of the Quad — India, Japan and Australia — in a show of resolve toward Beijing.
“Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable, and prosperous Indo-Pacific,” Trump said in the Philippines.
“We continue to protect peace through strength,” he added.

sources.news_title: Putin Slams Sanctions Ahead of Summit With Trump, Xi
sources.text:
President Vladimir Putin called Western sanctions on Russia a failure on Wednesday and met with his counterpart Xi Jinping in China ahead of their historic summit with US leader Donald Trump.
Thursday’s trilateral has triggered fears that the three powerful men could make decisions on the fate of Ukraine over the heads of Kyiv and Europe, and seek to carve up the world into 21st-century spheres of influence.
Washington had signalled that Ukraine — something Xi vehemently sees as not China’s problem — was not expected to be addressed, before Trump said that it would.
Putin, who met with Xi on Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen, was defiant on his war in Ukraine ahead of the three-man summit as he slammed Western sanctions provoked by the 2022 invasion.
“We see such examples in the failed attempts to isolate our country, Russia, which has faced unprecedented sanctions pressure,” Putin said.
After meeting the Russian leader, Xi urged closer ties with Moscow, saying the nations should “leverage the mechanisms for exchanges between the two countries’ governments, legislative bodies, militaries and political parties”.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, also in Shenzhen, said that sanctions on Russia “are going to continue to increase as long as this (Ukraine) war goes on.”
Also up for discussion in Thursday’s trilateral meeting are the Iran war and nuclear disarmament, according to Washington, after a US-Russia bilateral treaty on atomic weapons expired in February.
Beijing has long maintained that the US and Russia should reduce their giant nuclear arsenals before it agrees to talks on its smaller stockpile.
In From The Cold
Xi and Putin’s meeting on Wednesday, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting, was already their fifth this year, including one by video link.
Xi and Putin were expected to talk about energy and finance and then — in a smaller format — foreign policy, including Ukraine and North Korea, Russian officials said.
Earlier, Xi called for greater international cooperation on AI and free trade.
“Starting by lowering tariffs, expanding access and exploring regulations and management standards, China will conduct deep-seated reform,” Xi said as he opened the event.
Putin has been shunned by the West since launching Europe’s worst conflict since World War II with his 2022 attack on Ukraine.
Addressing the APEC gathering on Wednesday, he said he expected the trilateral summit to be “highly useful”.
“At a time when military-political risks are on the rise, what is desperately needed is unity rather than division… and dialogue rather than ultimatums,” Putin said.
Kim Incoming?
Trump landed in China on Wednesday after flying out of the Philippines, where a day earlier he met fellow leaders of the Quad — Australia, Japan and India — for the first time in his second term.
The grouping is broadly aimed at counterbalancing China’s regional influence.
He said he was eyeing one-on-one talks with Putin and Kim Jong Un at his next stop in Shenzhen, saying the North Korean leader “would like” to meet in China.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday stopped short of confirming the meeting with Kim.
“If we have a problem with North Korea, the only way we’re ever going to solve it is if we engage with them,” Rubio said in Manila.
Trump was in the Philippines for a summit of the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
His visit saw protests by around 2,000 people carrying banners reading “Trump out now” and “Reject Pax Silica” — a reference to a US supply chain initiative.
Tariffs, Chips And Rare Earths
While ASEAN leaders grappled with a raft of regional issues, the spectre of Trump’s ongoing tariff blitz has loomed large.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang on Monday slammed what he called a “countercurrent of unilateralism and protectionism” while touting Beijing’s own expanding trade with the bloc.
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Carney sang a similar tune on trade, with both explicitly citing a need to wean themselves off dependence on the US market.
On Tuesday, a combative Trump showed no let-up in his trade war with Beijing, saying the United States would catch China in rare-earths production “within 10 months”.
Hours before Trump touched down in Manila, Washington announced new rules on the transfer of advanced AI chips, a move that could potentially rankle ASEAN members.
Companies shipping high-end chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia will now require a special licence, as the countries were said to represent a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion”.
Singapore responded by saying it was now exploring ways to facilitate “trusted access” for firms based in the city-state.

sources.text:
US President Donald Trump has arrived in Shenzhen, southern China, for an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit set to end with the first three-way meeting between the leaders of the US, China and Russia. Chinese President Xi Jinping greeted him with a hug at the airport on November 18, returning a gesture Trump made during Xi’s state visit to Washington in September.
The trilateral with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin was scheduled for November 19 on the sidelines of the summit. Beijing said the three would discuss safeguarding world peace and strategic stability between the major powers.
Trump said he intended to raise ending Russia’s full-scale war in Ukraine. On November 17, he said he believed he was “very close to getting it done”.
Washington had earlier signalled that Ukraine would not be addressed, with nuclear arms control and the US war with Iran given priority. The last treaty limiting US and Russian nuclear arsenals expired in February and Beijing has insisted both powers cut their stockpiles before it joins any talks.
The summit came days after European envoys, EU and NATO officials were kept away from the main negotiating table at US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11. Kyiv has insisted that no settlement is possible without the European Union.
Xi held talks with Putin in Shenzhen on November 18, their fifth meeting this year. It was Putin’s first in-person appearance at an APEC leaders’ gathering since 2017.
Addressing business leaders, the Russian President condemned what he called instruments of economic dominance, including the sanctions imposed on Moscow after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. He said the Asia-Pacific accounted for more than half of Russia’s trade and that he wanted closer ties with the region.
Xi told executives the region needed more open trade and fairer growth. He pledged that China would cut tariffs, widen market access and reform its rules and standards.
Trump’s “America First” tariffs run counter to APEC’s long-standing goal of a Pacific Rim free trade zone. Although they were meant to curb China’s trade surplus, Beijing was on course to export about a trillion dollars more in goods than it imported for a second year running.
US curbs on Chinese access to advanced American technology, such as Nvidia’s artificial intelligence chips, remained a source of friction. Trump said he did not plan to raise Taiwan, a leading chipmaker, though he expected Xi to do so.
He also floated separate meetings with Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, neither of which had been confirmed when he landed.

sources.news_title: Putin-Trump-Xi: Three men, three different agendas
Trump, Xi, Putin hold historic trilateral meeting at APEC summit
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin convened for a historic trilateral meeting at the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, addressing critical global issues including nuclear arms reduction, artificial intelligence, and international stability.
Key Points
- US President Donald Trump received a grand welcome in Shenzhen from Chinese President Xi Jinping, including a rare personal reception at the airport.
- Trump, Xi, and Putin held an unprecedented trilateral meeting at the APEC summit to discuss global conflicts, nuclear arms reduction, and artificial intelligence.
- The White House confirmed Trump's intention to discuss nuclear weapons reduction, while Beijing has shown little enthusiasm for trilateral arms control.
- The meeting is seen as a significant diplomatic gain for all three leaders, boosting their international standing and influence.
- Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi also attended the APEC forum, with heightened bilateral tensions with China over her remarks on a Taiwan emergency.
US President Donald Trump arrived in China's high-tech city of Shenzhen to a grand welcome on Wednesday, with President Xi Jinping receiving him at the airport with a hug, a rare display of physical affection by the top Chinese leader.
In a reciprocal gesture to Trump's airport reception for him during his September visit to Washington, Xi personally welcomed the US president on the tarmac, marking the first such welcome by a Chinese leader since the founder of the People's Republic of China, Mao Zedong, greeted Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev nearly seven decades ago.
Trump arrived in Shenzhen from Manila to take part in the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting, which began on Wednesday, and an unprecedented trilateral meeting with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday.
In sharp contrast to Trump's high-profile reception, Putin was received earlier by Xi's close associate and powerful Standing Committee member of the ruling Communist Party Cai Qi, which Chinese officials said was also a rare gesture as the senior-most party leaders don't receive state guests at the airport.
Xi and Trump spent about 20 minutes exchanging pleasantries and watching the formations of Chinese J-10C fighter jets to welcome the US leader.
Historic Trilateral Discussions
Besides attending the gala dinner for the leaders of the 21st APEC summit on Wednesday, Trump, Xi and Putin will hold the trilateral meeting, the first-ever by leaders of the top three countries, to discuss a host of issues, including the Ukraine conflict, the Iran war as well as artificial intelligence and nuclear arms reduction.
Trump, Xi and Putin were seen having light-hearted banter at the dinner.
Work on the text of a statement to follow the trilateral meeting is proceeding intensively, Kremlin senior adviser Yuri Ushakov said, according to Russia's official TASS news agency.
Ushakov said the three leaders will discuss a wide range of issues, taking into account the global conflicts.
He also said they will discuss how major powers can build relationships and improve the global situation.
Tass also quoted Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov as saying that Putin has been invited to the G20 Summit in Miami next month, and the topic may be raised in his conversation with Trump at the APEC meeting.
Ahead of the meeting, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told the media on Monday that the three presidents will have an in-depth exchange of views on safeguarding world peace and enabling strategic stability in major-country relations.
"The summit is of ground-breaking significance", Mao said.
However, observers said that any concrete outcome from the first such trilateral meeting may be more symbolic.
Nuclear Arms and AI on the Agenda
The White House recently said that Trump will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons amid concerns over the future of global arms control following the expiry of the New START treaty between the US and Russia in February.
"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told the media.
Beijing has shown little enthusiasm for trilateral nuclear arms control, citing its far smaller arsenal than those of Washington and Moscow, and has repeatedly stressed that it does not subscribe to a model of great power co-governance in global affairs.
The discussions could also explore possible commitments on regulating the use of artificial intelligence in nuclear arsenals as part of a broader global governance agenda.
The three countries had engaged in weeks of discussions to finalise the agenda and protocol for the talks according to the media reports here. However, politically, the meeting was seen as a major gain for the three leaders.
Diplomatic Gains for Leaders
For Trump, the elaborate pomp and pageantry offered a grand diplomatic spectacle following a major setback in the midterm elections, in which his Republican Party suffered heavy losses to the Democrats in both the Senate and the House of Representatives.
For Xi, who is regarded as leader for life, it was a massive boost for his power and influence at home and abroad as he headed for a fourth five-year term in next year's once-in-a-five-year CPC congress.
For Putin, who suffered relative international isolation after he launched the Ukraine war, the trilateral meeting offered a most credible platform sharing table with Xi and Trump.
Speculation is also rife that North Korean leader Kim Jong-Un will visit Shenzhen to meet Trump.
Earlier, "old friends" Xi and Putin met in Shenzhen, their fourth meeting this year as the two leaders continue to coordinate their strategic positions opposing what they term US unilateral policies.
Xi described the China-Russia relations as 'unshakable as mountain' at their meeting, Russia's Tass news agency reported.
Xi told Putin that China and Russia must "firmly shoulder the responsibilities expected of major powers" and "lead and advance the multipolarisation of the world and the democratisation of international relations".

She said a few words to the Chinese leader, but Xi only smiled.
Chinese first lady Peng Liyuan also appears to say nothing to Takaichi beyond a greeting. After posing for a photograph, Xi and Takaichi exchanged nods as she walked away.
She may seek opportunities for informal brief conversation with Xi during her two-day stay in the southern Chinese city, having said she is "open" to dialogue with the Chinese side, Japanese news agency Kyodo reported.
Sino-Japanese ties have sharply deteriorated after Takaichi said in parliament in November last year that a Chinese attack on Taiwan, a self-ruled island that Beijing claims as its own, could lead Japan's Self-Defence Forces to support US forces.
Takaichi's remarks infuriated China and prompted it to take a series of political and economic retaliatory measures against Japan, including export restrictions on rare earths used in a wide range of high-tech products.
Several other APEC leaders, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, are attending the APEC summit.
The 21 APEC members included Australia, Brunei Darussalam, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, Peru, the Philippines, Russia, Singapore, Chinese Taipei, Thailand, the United States and Vietnam.

sources.news_title: Xi Jinping Breaks Protocol for Trump: China President's Airport Welcome Sparks Global Attention
sources.text:
Chinese President Xi Jinping personally welcomed U.S. President Donald Trump at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport on Wednesday, Nov. 18, in an unusual diplomatic gesture ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit and a planned trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Xi waited at the foot of Air Force One's stairs as Trump arrived in Shenzhen, Guangdong province.
The two leaders greeted each other before walking along a red carpet during a formal reception featuring Chinese and American flags. Xi's personal welcome marked a departure from customary diplomatic practice in China, where senior officials typically receive visiting foreign leaders at airports. The gesture highlighted the importance Beijing places on its relationship with Washington ahead of talks involving trade, security and international conflicts.
Xi's Airport Welcome for Trump Breaks Diplomatic Convention
Xi's reception of Trump stood out compared with the arrival of Putin earlier Wednesday. The Russian president was welcomed by Cai Qi, a member of China's Politburo Standing Committee and Xi's chief of staff, rather than Xi himself.
Trump's welcome also mirrored his own gesture toward Xi during the Chinese leader's U.S. visit in September, when Trump personally greeted him at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, and that reception was also considered unusual for a visiting head of state. The reciprocal gestures underscore the emphasis both leaders have placed on their personal relationship. However, the airport ceremonies alone don't indicate whether their upcoming talks will produce agreements.
Trump arrived in Shenzhen for the APEC summit, which China is hosting this year. The visit comes ahead of a planned trilateral meeting between Xi, Trump and Putin on Thursday, Nov. 19. The meeting is scheduled for 2:30 p.m. local time at Kylin Villa in Shenzhen, according to reports. It would bring together the leaders of China, the United States and Russia to discuss major international issues. China confirmed the meeting earlier this week, but officials haven't publicly outlined a detailed agenda.
Trump is expected to raise nuclear weapons reduction, while U.S. officials have indicated that the Iran conflict could also be discussed. Russia's war in Ukraine is another issue expected to feature, although Beijing has maintained that European countries should be involved in discussions concerning the conflict.
The talks come as the three countries navigate trade disputes, military security and competing geopolitical interests. Officials haven't announced that the meeting will produce a joint agreement or formal commitments.
Trump and Putin Initiated the Trilateral Talks
The idea of a trilateral meeting was discussed by Trump and Putin during a phone call in September, according to Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov. The possibility of holding a three-way meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit was subsequently raised. The White House and Kremlin confirmed plans for the meeting in November, setting the stage for the gathering in Shenzhen.
The proposed format would bring together leaders of three major powers with competing interests on several geopolitical issues. Discussions involving Ukraine, Iran, nuclear weapons or trade could have implications beyond their bilateral relationships, although the scope of the talks remains unclear.
APEC Summit Focuses on Trade and Regional Cooperation
The broader APEC summit agenda includes economic cooperation, trade, supply chains, artificial intelligence and energy. The gathering brings regional leaders together to discuss economic priorities across the Asia-Pacific.
The summit also gives China an opportunity to showcase Shenzhen, a major technology and manufacturing centre in Guangdong province. Trump's visit marks his second trip to China in 2026, following a state visit to Beijing in May. His latest visit comes as Washington and Beijing continue to manage trade disputes and competition over technology and strategic interests.

sources.news_title: Trump Arrives in China, Set to Meet Putin, Xi
sources.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump arrived in China on Nov. 18, a day ahead of his highly anticipated trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
Xi welcomed Trump at Shenzhen Bao’an International Airport in the southern Chinese tech hub, where Beijing is hosting the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, a gathering of 21 economies across the region.
On the sidelines of the APEC summit, Trump is also scheduled to hold a bilateral meeting with Xi on Thursday, local time.
Trump also held a bilateral meeting with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., during which he said Washington was expanding its defense cooperation with its treaty ally and suggested working with Manila on a major civilian nuclear energy project. At a subsequent state luncheon, Trump said the two countries had just concluded a major trade deal.
The Philippine presidential office later said the two sides had reached an understanding on areas of economic cooperation, without mentioning a trade deal, and Jose Manuel Romualdez, the Philippine ambassador to the United States, said nothing had been signed.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump called the trade deal “a true landmark,” and said it would be great for U.S. farmers and those in the energy sector.
Before Trump’s arrival, Xi and Putin both delivered speeches at the opening ceremony of the APEC CEO summit on Wednesday, local time.
In his speech, Putin said he expected a “big potential benefit” from Thursday’s trilateral summit.
Xi said in his speech that China remains committed to seeking cooperation, including under the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), which is a Chinese foreign policy aiming to build geopolitical clout by financing infrastructure projects throughout Southeast Asia, Africa, and Europe.
Putin and Xi also held a bilateral talk on Wednesday, local time. According to Russia’s state-run news agency TASS, the two leaders talked for more than two hours and discussed “prospects for further economic cooperation” between the two neighboring countries.
Guo Jiakun, spokesperson of China’s foreign ministry, said during a daily briefing on Wednesday that the three leaders would “have an in-depth exchange of views on important issues bearing on global peace.”
Heather Williams, director of the Project on Nuclear Issues and senior fellow at the Washington-based think tank Center for Strategic and International Studies, expressed low expectations for the three-way summit in a video posted on social media platform X on Nov. 17.
“An ambitious denuclearization deal seems pretty unlikely to come out of this potential trilateral meeting. China has been a little bit nervous, it seems, about whether or not they should even participate in this meeting. The reason for that is that China has consistently said that they aren’t ready for the types of arms control that the U.S. and the Soviet Union, and then the U.S. and Russia, did,” Williams said.
“So, just the fact that these three are meeting and might talk about nuclear issues—it could be a little too much for Beijing.
“The other reason is Russia. Russia has a pretty poor track record of compliance with arms control agreements. They haven’t shown a lot of interest in new arms control in recent years, and, to be clear, Vladimir Putin is really just interested in the war in Ukraine right now.”
Williams also said ending without an agreement isn’t a failure and that the meeting itself is “a step forward.”
Trump will return to the United States after his visit to China.

sources.text:
Russia’s president Vladimir Putin has told global business leaders assembled in China that sanctions and efforts to contain Russia would only hurt western powers, as he advocated a “larger Eurasian partnership”.
Putin said that “formerly dominant powers” were trying to “hold back the development of those who show success and progress”, according to an English translation provided by his Chinese hosts at the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation in Shenzhen on Wednesday.
The Russian president argued that “unprecedented” sanctions against his country following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 had only strengthened Moscow’s economy at the expense of others, particularly the EU.
Leaders are gathering in the southern Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen for what is expected to be a week of high-stakes diplomacy in Asia, culminating in a trilateral meeting between Putin, Chinese leader Xi Jinping and US president Donald Trump on Thursday.

Putin’s address to chief executives at a forum held on the sidelines of the Apec leaders’ meeting offered a rare opportunity for the Russian president to speak directly to global corporate figures at a time when Moscow has been marginalised and the country’s businesses have faced sanctions over his war in Ukraine.
In his own keynote to executives earlier on Wednesday, Xi warned against “rampant” protectionism, remarks seen as an implicit criticism of the US ahead of an expected separate bilateral meeting with Trump.
Tensions between the two countries have mounted this week over new export controls on chips and US frustration with Beijing’s rare earth restrictions.
“Today, we find ourselves in a changing and turbulent world,” Xi said. “Global growth lacks momentum, and unilateralism and protectionism are rampant.”
“Still, global trade keeps growing against headwinds,” he added, saying that China would cut tariffs and welcome foreign investment.
The venue appeared noticeably emptier for Putin than during Xi’s speech. Several attendees confirmed that many had left after Xi’s talk.
The Russian president railed against European powers, who he said “have decided to stop the supply of Russian energy resources that have established the [prosperity] of the European Union for decades”.
He added that the EU was suffering from budget deficits, rising debt, inflation and a declining industrial base. He touted economic agreements across the Middle East, Africa and Asia, including with China and Indonesia, which he described as a “Russian project to establish a larger Eurasian partnership”.
Putin’s speech came after Japan’s defence ministry said that two suspected Russian planes had violated its airspace near the southern islands of Okinawa in the early hours of Tuesday.
Taiwan’s defence ministry said that it had tracked two “Russian military aircraft” in its Air Defence Identification Zone off its eastern coast around the same time. South Korea also said several aircraft had entered its identification zone, according to local media.
The Apec leaders’ summit brings together officials and executives from 21 member economies representing about 60 per cent of global economic output.
The CEO forum would include about 2,000 executives, organisers have said, with representatives from 115 Fortune 500 companies.
US business leaders in attendance included Michael Miebach of Mastercard, Ryan McInerney of Visa and Carol B Tomé of UPS, alongside Chinese executives such as BYD’s Wang Chuanfu, Lei Jun of Xiaomi, Wang Xingxing of robot maker Unitree, CATL founder Robin Zeng, ZTE chair Fang Rong and Robin Li, chief executive of Baidu. Boeing’s global president also participated.

“Beijing wants these participants to leave believing that engagement with China remains essential to their prosperity,” said Han Shen Lin, China managing director The Asia Group.

sources.news_title: Xi says Asia-Pacific needs open trade and Putin condemns sanctions as Trump arrives in China – WTOP News
sources.text:
SHENZHEN, China (AP) — The Asia-Pacific must pursue more open trade and equitable growth if it is to remain stable and dynamic, Chinese President Xi Jinping told business executives gathered Wednesday in the southern Chinese technology and financial hub of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
U.S. President Donald Trump arrived Wednesday for the APEC leaders’ summit, traveling from the Philippines, where he attended an annual summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.
Trump’s “America First” approach of tariff hikes and other moves runs counter to APEC’s aim of eventually forming a Pacific Rim free trade zone. U.S. limits on Chinese access to leading-edge American technology, such as the Nvidia computer chips that help to power artificial intelligence, are a constant source of strain with Beijing.
Xi and other APEC leaders called for a more open approach, without directly criticizing the U.S. shift toward protecting its own markets.
APEC summit venue showcases China’s central role in trade
The summit is showcasing Shenzhen, which China has transformed in the past four decades from a fishing village into a skyscraper-studded center for export manufacturing and technology. China’s ascent as the second-largest economy hinged on global investments and access to world markets as global manufacturers shifted factories overseas to tap into cheaper labor and faster-growing markets.
“China will not only cut tariffs and expand market access, but also go a step further. We will carry out reform in challenging areas such as rules, regulation, and standards,” Xi told the CEO summit, reiterating Beijing’s pledges to improve conditions for global investors.
“While pursuing its own development, China has shared opportunities with other countries and worked for common development,” he said. “It has steadily brought stability and predictability to world economic growth and international trade and economic cooperation.”
Xi’s speech highlighted China’s aim to lead global industrial transformation, said George Chen, partner and chair of Digital Practice at The Asia Group.
“While he didn’t say so explicitly, his message was clear: China wants to be seen as a partner in global technology development, in contrast to Washington’s more restrictive approach,” Chen said, noting that Xi did not mention export controls, Nvidia or the U.S. directly.
Pressures lie behind the pomp and positivity over open trade
Xi faces pressure at home from slowing growth as retail spending and investment have dragged as China endures a prolonged property market slump. The economy is still growing at a rate of more than 4%, but that’s mainly due to surging exports that are provoking a backlash among many of China’s trading partners. China’s trade surplus for this year is on track to exceed $1 trillion for a second year in a row.
Still, Trump’s emphasis on friendly relations with Xi may lead to an extension of the trade truce reached last year after a series of tariff escalations.
Friction with Washington over higher U.S. tariffs and other trade barriers is leading to realignments among other trading partners. On Tuesday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney met with Xi and they agreed to cut tariffs on each other’s goods. Carney has cultivated tighter economic ties with China and the European Union in response to strains in Canada’s relationship with Trump.
“Canada is undergoing a transformation of our own. We are turning global uncertainty into national opportunity in a more dangerous and divided world,” Carney told the CEO summit. “Canada is choosing a path towards a stronger, more prosperous, more resilient future.”
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim told the executives of top Chinese and multinational companies that bigger economies should recognize that fair and dynamic growth benefits all.
“Countries cannot impose their position, their own peculiar circumstances, to countries to decide,” Anwar said. “They must accept that countries must emerge, focus on trade and investments, because that would ultimately benefit their people.”
Putin takes aim at sanctions, says Asia-Pacific is vital for Russia
Russian President Vladimir Putin took aim at “instruments of economic dominance,” such as the sanctions imposed following the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
“Sanctions, tariffs, and export restrictions” have “outlived their usefulness and have largely lost their intimidating effect,” Putin told the CEO summit in his first in-person appearance at an APEC leaders meeting since 2017.
He highlighted his country’s desire to cultivate closer economic ties with the Asia-Pacific, saying the region accounts for more than half of its total trade.
Russia has submitted a bid to chair APEC in 2035, Putin said.
The 21 APEC economies account for 60% of global economic activity, half of global trade and 40% of humanity. The leaders will meet behind closed doors on Thursday, while holding other meetings on the event’s sidelines. That will include a “trilateral” encounter between Trump, Putin and Xi, the first such summit between those three global powers.
APEC does not take binding decisions, but over 37 years it has served as a forum for building a consensus on cooperation and more open trade.
“The decisions we, and particularly you take today, individually and collectively, will determine whether the APEC region and the international community continue to be a source of dynamism, stability and opportunity in an increasingly uncertain world,” Anwar said.
___
Associated Press writer Kanis Leung in Hong Kong contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Putin and Trump meet in Shenzhen, their first talks since Alaska summit
sources.text:
(RAHNUMA) :Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump shook hands in Shenzhen on Wednesday, their first meeting since their Alaska summit in August 2025, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
The encounter came after Putin began talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping, and a day before a historic three-way meeting between the three leaders in the southern Chinese city.
The trilateral summit has raised fears that the leaders could make decisions about Ukraine over the heads of Kyiv and Europe, and divide the world into new spheres of influence. Washington initially signaled that Ukraine might not be discussed, but Trump later said it would be on the agenda.
Russian officials said Xi and Putin were expected to discuss energy and finance, followed by talks on foreign policy, including Ukraine and North Korea, in a smaller format. The meeting is their fifth this year.
Xi called for closer exchanges between the two countries’ governments, parliaments, militaries and political parties, and stressed the need for international cooperation on artificial intelligence and free trade.
Putin criticized Western sanctions imposed after Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, saying they had failed to stop Russia’s growth. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who is also in Shenzhen, said sanctions would be stepped up as long as the war continued.
Trump arrived from the Philippines, where he attended a summit with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, and said he wanted to hold separate one-on-one meetings with Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio did not confirm any details of a possible meeting with Kim.
Trade tensions also hung over the summit. Trump pledged that the US would match China’s rare-earths production within 10 months, while Chinese Premier Li Qiang criticized protectionism and highlighted China’s growing trade with ASEAN.
